# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XVII. A DOUBLE VICTORY

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

On the initial Sunday of November, Lionel Fairlie attended church, creating every bit of the stir he wished for. Upon the steps of the church, Mr. Ashdown distractedly shook his hand, expressing a vague hope that Mrs. Fairlie was in good health.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0000 }

“Though her condition was poor prior to her interment by me a decade back, her well-being has likely improved since,” roared Lionel, startling and entertaining all present save Mr. Ashdown, who was preoccupied with considering whether he had rendered his sermon's final point as lucidly as possible, remaining entirely unaware of what passed between himself and Lionel.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0001 }

Lionel stopped Grace as she reached the gate.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0002 }

“I maintained my promise, as you can observe—maintained my promise, Red Rose. From this moment until December's initial Sunday, I am liberated. Excellent discourse, young lady—excellent discourse. The thoughts within your father's mind surpass what his facial expression reveals. However, he made a single self-contradiction—inform him that he contradicted himself. Furthermore, inform him of my desire for that brimstone sermon come December. A marvelous method to conclude the former year—experiencing a flavor of hell, as you are aware. Plus, what would be wrong with a pleasing, savory message regarding heaven to begin the New Year? Even if it would lack half the interest of hell, young lady—not even half. Nevertheless, I would care to discover your father's perspective concerning heaven—he possesses the ability to think—the most unusual trait on earth—an individual possessing the capacity to think. Still, he truly did contradict himself. Ha, ha! This presents an inquiry you could pose to him at some point when he is not sleeping, young lady. ‘Can God make a stone so big He couldn’t lift it Himself?’ Avoid forgetting this moment. I desire to listen to his judgment regarding the matter. I have bewildered numerous clergymen using that very thought, young lady.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0003 }

Grace was pleased to break away from him and hurry back to her house. Dan Coyle, who was positioned in the midst of the gathering of boys near the gate, cast his eyes upon her and formed his lips into "pig-girl," though he did not venture to pronounce the words out loud in that particular spot. The following day at school proved to be a different story. During the midday break, Grace met Dan within the small grove of spruces located at the rear of the schoolhouse, and Dan yelled again,
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0004 }

“Pig-girl! Pig-girl! Rooster-girl!”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0005 }

Rising abruptly from a mossy cushion behind a small cluster of fir trees, where he had been engrossed in reading, Edmund Carrow stood up. Although his face was extremely pale, a fiery light blazed in his eyes.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0006 }

“You keep quiet, Dan Coyle!” he commanded.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0007 }

“Oh, hello, Miss Edmund,” Dan answered back, completely unconcerned. He jumped lightly up onto the top of the rail fence and sang out mockingly,
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0008 }

“Mustard pot thief, Yellow-bellied coward, Mustard pot thief!”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0009 }

“A coincidence is what you are!” Edmund exclaimed with disdain, his face growing even paler. Although he possessed merely a vague notion of a coincidence's definition, Dan was completely ignorant of the term and assumed it was an exceptionally insulting remark.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0010 }

“Bah! Sissy!” he shouted once more. “The things your mother writes are untruths—untruths—untruths! Likewise, Grace Ashdown is a swine-girl—a—swine-girl—a swine-girl! Furthermore, she is a fowl-girl—a fowl-girl—a fowl-girl! Bah! Sissy—sissy—custard—”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0011 }

Dan was unable to say anything more. Launching himself over the distance between them, Edmund delivered a single, precise hit that sent Dan tumbling backward off the fence. This abrupt, humiliating fall from Dan was met by Grace with an explosion of laughter and applauding hands. Turning red with fury, Dan leaped to his feet and started scaling the fence again. At that precise moment, however, the school bell sounded, and Dan was well aware of the consequences for pupils who arrived late under Mr. Hazard’s authority.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0012 }

“This will be fought to the end,” he bellowed. “Yellow-belly!”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0013 }

“Whenever you wish,” Edmund replied.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0014 }

“Oh, no, no, Edmund,” Grace objected. “Do not battle him. What he states does not bother me—I would not stoop to care about someone such as him.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0015 }

“You were insulted by him, and my mother was insulted by him as well,” Edmund said, maintaining that very same lethal composure. “Dan, tonight following school.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0016 }

“Dad says I have to head straight back from school to gather potatoes behind the harrows,” Dan replied sullenly. “However, tomorrow evening will work.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0017 }

“Very well—in this place tomorrow evening,” Edmund concurred.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0018 }

“And your effeminate face will be crushed by me,” Dan pledged.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0019 }

Edmund trembled—less out of dread regarding the menace than from disgust at its grossness and crude nature. Even so, he kept his chin up and walked forward into the building. Grace walked behind him, her feelings torn. It pained her to imagine Edmund coming to blows with that petty worm, yet oh, how magnificent he had been! Furthermore, his battle was for her—Grace Ashdown—so that her defamer would be punished! Naturally, triumph would be his—those eyes guaranteed success.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0020 }

By the time evening arrived, Grace felt somewhat less confident in her champion, though. Throughout the remainder of the school day, Edmund had appeared remarkably silent and uninteresting.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0021 }

“Were Kit the sole concern,” she breathed in a sigh to Ida, while the two rested atop the tombstone of Hezekiah Pollock within the cemetery. “Being such a combatant—Dan would be dispatched by him quickly. Edmund, however, lacks expertise in combat.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0022 }

“I am terribly fearful that he will suffer injury,” Ida uttered with a sigh, as she detested conflict and was unable to comprehend the quiet, hidden delight that she sensed within Grace.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0023 }

“He shouldn’t be,” Grace stated uneasily. “His size is completely equal to Dan’s.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0024 }

“However, Dan is a lot older,” Ida remarked. “Indeed, he is almost twelve months older.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0025 }

“When you actually add it all up, Dan hasn't fought very much,” Grace remarked. “I think he is actually a coward. He never expected Edmund to fight, otherwise he would not have resorted to name-calling in his presence. Oh, Ida, if you had only been able to see Edmund’s face as he glared at him! It gave me a shiver—a pleasant kind of shiver. He resembled Sir Galahad so much from the poem father read aloud to us this past Saturday.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0026 }

“The idea of their battle repulses me, and I would be glad if it could be prevented,” Ida remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0027 }

“Oh, now it must proceed,” exclaims Grace. “A point of honour is involved. Ida, do not you venture to inform a soul. Should you do so, I will refrain from ever sharing secrets with you in the future!”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0028 }

“I will keep quiet,” Ida assented. “However, I am not remaining tomorrow to witness the brawl. My return home will be immediate.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0029 }

“Oh, very well. I must attend—it would be unkind to refrain, since Edmund is battling on my behalf. I shall fasten my colours upon his sleeve—that is the proper custom when he serves as my knight. What good fortune that Mrs. Carrow presented me with that lovely blue hair-ribbon on my birthday! Having been worn merely twice, it remains nearly fresh. However, I desire certainty regarding Edmund's victory. Should he lose, it will prove so—so embarrassing.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0030 }

Had Grace been able to behold her defender at that moment, her skepticism would have grown. Returning from school, Edmund found that his noble fury had dwindled, leaving a highly unpleasant sensation in its stead. The following evening held a match against Dan Coyle—an event he dreaded—as the mere idea filled him with aversion. Furthermore, the anticipation haunted him continuously. He was unable to escape the lingering thought for even a single second. Would the pain be severe? A dreadful fear possessed him that the agony would be great. Moreover, was he destined to suffer defeat and disgrace?
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0031 }

An inability to consume any notable amount of supper affected him. Although Tabitha had baked a large quantity of monkey-faces, which were his favorite, a single one was all he could force down his throat. Four were consumed by Kit. Such an appetite baffled Edmund. What allowed anyone to eat? Furthermore, in what way were they able to converse so cheerfully as they currently did? Mother was present, her cheeks pink and her eyes bright. That her son was required to fight on the following day remained unknown to her. Darkly, Edmund pondered whether her gaiety would persist if she were aware. Tabitha’s photograph had been captured by Kit using his new camera, and after the outcome was circulated around the table, Tabitha became intensely outraged by it.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0032 }

“I am not attractive, Mrs. Dr. dear, and I am fully aware of it, and I have forever been aware of it,” she declared with a hurt expression, “yet I shall never, no, never accept that I am as unattractive as I appear in that image.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0033 }

Kit found humor in this, prompting Nell to join him in laughter once more. Unable to bear it any longer, Edmund stood up and ran away to his room.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0034 }

“Mrs. Dr. dear, that child has something weighing on his mind,” Tabitha remarked. “Hardly anything has been eaten by him. Could he be planning yet another poem, do you think?”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0035 }

At that moment, poor Edmund’s mind was completely detached from the celestial domain of poetry. He rested an elbow on the open sill of his window and let his head drop heavily into his hands.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0036 }

“Edmund, come down to the shore with me,” shouted Kit, bursting inside. “To-night, the boys intend to burn the grass on the sand-hill. We have permission from Father to go. Come on.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0037 }

Under different circumstances, Edmund would have been thrilled, as he took great pleasure in the combustion of the sand-hill grass. On this occasion, however, he adamantly declined to attend, remaining steadfast against all persuasion and pleading. Disheartened, Kit disliked the prospect of making the lengthy, pitch-black trek to Seven Gulls Point by himself, so he withdrew to his museum located in the attic and became absorbed in a volume. His sense of letdown quickly evaporated while he delighted in the exploits of ancient romantic figures, periodically stopping to envision himself as a renowned commander guiding his soldiers to triumph upon a momentous battleground.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0038 }

Edmund remained sitting by his window up to his bedtime. Izzy entered quietly, wishing to learn what was troubling him, but Edmund was unable to speak about the matter, even with Izzy. Discussing it appeared to lend it a truth that made him pull back. Merely pondering it brought sufficient agony. On the maple trees beyond his window, the dry, brittle leaves made a rustling sound. Within the sunken, silvery sky, the radiant rose and fiery colors had faded, and above Fern Hollow, the full moon mounted grandly. Far in the distance, past the hills, a glowing woodfire was creating a splendid display across the skyline. The night was crisp and luminous, allowing distant noises to be perceived clearly. Across the pond, a fox barked; down at the Glen station, an engine puffed; inside the maple grove, a blue-jay shrieked wildly; and over on the manse lawn, laughter could be heard. In what way could people laugh? In what way could foxes, blue-jays, and engines carry on as though the next day held no impending event?
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0039 }

“Oh, how I long for it to end,” Edmund moaned.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0040 }

That night brought him very little sleep, and he struggled greatly to swallow his morning porridge. Tabitha had been quite generous with her servings. That day, Mr. Hazard discovered that he was an unpromising student. Grace Ashdown appeared to have her thoughts wandering as well. On his slate, Dan Coyle continually sketched covert drawings of girls featuring heads of pigs or roosters, displaying them for everyone's view. Word regarding the approaching fight had spread, leading the majority of the boys and a large number of the girls to gather in the spruce plantation by the time Dan and Edmund went there following school. Ida had departed for home, yet Grace remained present, after tying her blue ribbon about Edmund’s arm. Edmund felt grateful that Kit, Izzy, and Bess were not included in the group of onlookers. For some reason, they had failed to learn about the upcoming event and had likewise returned home. Edmund stood before Dan with complete courage at this point. In the final instant, his entire dread had disappeared, though he remained disgusted by the prospect of a brawl. It was observed that Dan was actually paler beneath his freckles than Edmund was. A command was issued by one of the elder boys, and Dan punched Edmund in the face.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0041 }

Edmund staggered slightly. For an instant, the stinging hurt from the strike radiated across his entire delicate body. Afterwards, he ceased to feel any agony. An unfamiliar sensation, unlike anything he had previously known, appeared to wash over him in a great wave. A deep red glow covered his face, and his eyes blazed such as fire. The students at Glen St. Agnes school had never imagined that “Miss Edmund” was capable of appearing in such a manner. He threw his weight onward and engaged Dan in a fight like a youthful wildcat.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0042 }

In the brawls of the boys at the Glen school, no specific regulations existed. One had to grab wherever possible and land punches by any means. Edmund engaged with a fierce rage and a delight in the clash that proved too much for Dan to maintain his footing against. The entire affair concluded extremely fast. Edmund possessed no lucid awareness of his actions until, all at once, the crimson fog vanished from his vision, revealing him on top of the lying form of Dan, whose nose—what a terrible thing!—was gushing blood.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0043 }

“Have you had plenty?” asked Edmund with his teeth pressed together.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0044 }

Dan glumly acknowledged that he had done so.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0045 }

“Does my mother write what is not true?”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0046 }

“No.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0047 }

“Is Grace Ashdown not a pig-girl?”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0048 }

“No.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0049 }

“Or a rooster-girl?”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0050 }

“No.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0051 }

“And am I no coward?”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0052 }

“No.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0053 }

Edmund was about to inquire, “And you are a liar?” yet compassion stepped in, preventing him from causing Dan any more embarrassment. What is more, the sight of that blood was dreadful.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0054 }

“You may leave, in that case,” he said scornfully.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0055 }

A noisy applause came from the youths sitting atop the rail fence, yet a few of the girls wept. Fear had overtaken them. Schoolboy brawls were familiar to them, but none matched Edmund when he had wrestled Dan. An element of horror had surrounded him. They believed Dan would be slain by him. With everything concluded, their weeping grew hysterical—with the exception of Grace, who remained motionless, her cheeks flushed red.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0056 }

Edmund did not linger to receive the reward of a victor. Leaping across the fence, he hurried down the spruce-covered hill toward Fern Hollow. No triumphant delight filled him, yet he experienced a quiet contentment from completing his duty and redeeming his honor—blended with a nauseating shudder whenever he recalled the bloody nose of Dan. Its appearance had been dreadful, and Edmund detested dreadful things.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0057 }

Additionally, it started to dawn on him that his own body was rather bruised and aching. A cut caused his lip to swell, while a peculiar sensation affected one of his eyes. Within Fern Hollow, he met Mr. Ashdown, who was returning from a visit made that afternoon to the Miss Ainslies. Upon seeing him, that reverend gentleman gave him a serious look.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0058 }

“You appear to have been in a fight, Edmund, do you not?”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0059 }

“Yes, sir,” Edmund replied, anticipating a reprimand.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0060 }

“What was the topic?”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0061 }

“Dan Coyle claimed that my mother penned falsehoods and that Grace was nothing more than a swine-herd,” replied Edmund without hesitation.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0062 }

“Oh—h! In that case, Edmund, your actions were unquestionably warranted.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0063 }

“Is it your opinion that fighting is proper, sir?” Edmund inquired with curiosity.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0064 }

“Not constantly—and not frequently—yet on occasion—indeed, on occasion,” stated John Ashdown. “Whenever women are disrespected for example—like with you. My principle, Edmund, is, refrain from fighting until you are certain that you should, and after that apply every bit of your strength to it. Regardless of various bruises I gather that you emerged victorious.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0065 }

“Indeed, I forced him to retract everything he said.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0066 }

“Extremely well done—truly, extremely well done. It hadn't occurred to me that you possessed such a combative spirit, Edmund.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0067 }

“Prior to this, I had never engaged in combat—and until the very end, I wished to avoid it—and after that,” stated Edmund, resolved to confess everything fully, “I found enjoyment in it during the time I was doing it.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0068 }

A twinkle shone in the Rev. John’s eyes.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0069 }

“Were you—initially—a bit scared?”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0070 }

“I felt extremely scared,” sincere Edmund remarked. “However, I do not intend to feel scared again, sir. Experiencing fear about troubles is more unpleasant than those troubles are. I plan to request that father drive me to Kettlebridge tomorrow so I can have my tooth pulled.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0071 }

“You are correct once more. ‘Fear is more pain than is the pain it fears.’ Are you aware of who penned those words, Edmund? William Shakespeare was the author. Did that extraordinary individual fail to understand a single sentiment, feeling, or trial of the human soul? Upon your return home, inform your mother that I feel pride in you.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0072 }

Edmund refrained from informing her of that, nevertheless; yet he recounted everything else to her, and she felt for him and expressed her pleasure that he had defended her and Grace, and she applied ointment to his tender places and applied cologne to his throbbing head.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0073 }

“Is every mother as kind as you are?” Edmund inquired, embracing her tightly. “Defending you is truly worth it.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0074 }

Nell descended the stairs to find Miss Winifred and Tabitha in the living room, where they took great pleasure in hearing the account. Tabitha was especially delighted.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0075 }

“I am exceedingly pleased to learn he put up a fine struggle, dear Mrs. Dr. It might possibly strip him of those foolish poetic notions. Moreover, I never, no, never was able to stand that tiny viper known as Dan Coyle. Won't you move your seat closer to the hearth, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr? The nights in November are quite cold.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0076 }

“I appreciate it, Tabitha, but coldness isn't a problem for me. Prior to arriving here, I stopped by the manse and warmed up considerably—even if doing so required me to enter the kitchen, seeing as every other room lacked a fire. Take my word for it, that kitchen appeared to have been tossed around with a rod. Mr. Ashdown was absent from the house. Discovering his whereabouts proved impossible for me, yet I suspect he was visiting the Ainslies' place. Would you believe, my dear Nell, rumor has it that his visits there have occurred often throughout the entire autumn, leading folks to suspect his intentions involve courting Clementine.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0077 }

“If Clementine became his bride, he’d gain a truly wonderful partner,” remarked Nell, placing more driftwood upon the flames. “Among all the young women I have met, she is exceptionally lovely—a genuine member of Joseph’s lineage.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0078 }

“Ye—s—except she belongs to the Episcopal church,” Miss Winifred remarked with hesitation. “Naturally, that surpasses her being a Methodist—nevertheless, it seems to me Mr. Ashdown might discover a sufficiently suitable spouse within his own fold. Still, the rumor might well be groundless. Just one month back, I remarked to him, ‘It is time you took another wife, Mr. Ashdown.’ His expression grew as appalled as though my proposal had been indecent. ‘The woman I married rests in the cemetery, Mrs. Kerr,’ he replied, employing his usual mild and holy tone. ‘That is my assumption,’ I responded, ‘otherwise I should not be recommending another marriage to you.’ At that, his countenance appeared even more scandalized. Because of this, I question whether this Clementine account holds much truth. Whenever an unmarried clergyman visits a home containing an unmarried female on two occasions, every gossip claims he is pursuing her.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0079 }

“In my opinion—should I be bold enough to utter it—Mr. Ashdown possesses too much shyness to seek a second wife in courtship,” Tabitha stated gravely.
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0080 }

“Trust me, he isn’t timid,” Miss Winifred fired back. “Yes, he is forgetful, but he is certainly not timid. Despite his daydreaming and preoccupation, he holds himself in high regard, as men do, and once he fully pays attention, he wouldn't consider it much trouble to propose to any lady. No, the problem stems from him fooling himself that his heart is in the grave, even though it continues to pump inside him as everyone else's does. Whether he holds a fancy for Clementine Ainslie remains uncertain. Should that be the case, we have to accept it gracefully. She possesses a sweet nature, manages a home well, and would be a splendid mother to those unfortunate, overlooked children. Besides,” Miss Winifred finished with a tone of resignation, “an Episcopalian was what my grandmother happened to be.”
{: #nw-v05-c17-p0081 }
